text: Platt scaling maps a classifier's score to a probability through a two-parameter sigmoid fitted by maximum likelihood, and the fit should use data not used to train the classifier because training-set outputs are biased.
Isotonic-regression calibration, which fits a non-decreasing step function to the classifier's scores, was introduced for classifier calibration by Zadrozny and Elkan.
Zadrozny and Elkan (2001) obtained calibrated probabilities from naive Bayes by binning and from decision trees by smoothing and curtailment, studied on the KDD'98 dataset.

On eight binary problems, Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005) found logistic regression and bagged trees well calibrated without post-hoc calibration, and post-calibration did not help them on most problems.

Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005) found random forests well calibrated on some problems but not on five of their eight, with predictions pushed away from 0 and 1 and sigmoid-shaped reliability plots, which they attribute to averaging high-variance trees.

In the learning curves of Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005), Platt scaling beat isotonic regression when the calibration set had fewer than about 200 to 1000 cases, and isotonic regression did as well as or better than Platt scaling with 1000 or more.
Boosted trees trained with the exponential loss produce sigmoid-shaped distortions in their predicted probabilities, and Platt scaling or isotonic regression substantially reduce their cross-entropy.

In a comparison of ten learners on eleven binary problems, random forests, bagged trees and neural nets gave the best probabilities before calibration, and calibrated boosted trees the best after calibration.
On 34 UCI datasets, isotonic regression slightly worsened the Brier score of random forests of probability-estimation trees and Platt scaling gave a limited improvement.

On 18 consumer-credit datasets, Fonseca and Lopes (2017) found that Platt scaling gave almost no improvement to logistic regression, while isotonic regression improved it in more than 75% of cases, and that random forests gained more from calibration than gradient boosting.

A benchmark of 21 classifiers on 30 binary TabArena datasets found that Platt scaling and isotonic regression can degrade proper scoring performance for strong modern tabular models, and that no calibration method dominates uniformly.

On 104 binary tabular datasets with tuned classical and neural models (logistic regression, random forests, gradient-boosted trees and others), no post-hoc calibration method consistently improved over the uncalibrated model, and Platt scaling on probabilities and binning-based methods degraded performance.

Because post-hoc calibration cannot reduce refinement error, the change in a proper score such as the Brier score before and after calibration measures the calibration gain net of any loss in discrimination.
Expected calibration error partitions predictions into M equally spaced bins and averages the gap between accuracy and confidence across bins, weighted by the number of samples in each bin.
Binned estimates of calibration error are biased and depend on the number of bins and how they are formed. Equal-mass bins have lower bias than equal-width bins.
A binned calibration-error estimate can underestimate the calibration error of methods with continuous outputs such as Platt scaling.
Binned ECE favours binning-based calibration functions and ignores refinement error, so a method can lower ECE while degrading the overall quality of the predictions.
The ranking of recalibration methods can change sharply with the choice of calibration measure.
On raw scores, the logistic calibration family does not include the identity map, so logistic calibration can uncalibrate a classifier that is already well calibrated.
Strictly proper scoring rules such as the logarithmic and quadratic (Brier) scores reward honest probability forecasts.
CORP reliability diagrams, based on isotonic regression via the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm, are statistically consistent and reproducible, unlike diagrams that depend on ad hoc binning.
Reliability diagrams plot the observed frequency of the positive class against the mean predicted probability in bins of predicted probability.

In scikit-learn's CalibratedClassifierCV the default ensemble=True fits one classifier and one calibrator per cross-validation split, whereas an already fitted classifier can be calibrated on separate data by wrapping it in FrozenEstimator.
Isotonic calibration introduces ties in predicted probabilities and can therefore change ROC-AUC, whereas sigmoid calibration is strictly monotonic and preserves ranking.
The experiments use scikit-learn.
Silva Filho et al. (2023) survey how to assess and improve classifier calibration, including proper scoring rules, visualisation and post-hoc calibration methods.
Before any recalibration, random forests and gradient boosting had lower test-set Brier scores than logistic regression on most of the 18 credit datasets studied by Fonseca and Lopes (2017).

In Manokhin and Grønhaug's expected log-loss ranks over 30 TabArena datasets and five folds, isotonic recalibration improved the rank of random forests but worsened the ranks of scikit-learn's GradientBoostingClassifier and HistGradientBoostingClassifier, and Platt scaling ranked ahead of isotonic regression for all three tree models.

In Manokhin and Grønhaug's per-dataset results (30 TabArena datasets, five folds, default hyperparameters, calibration split taken from the training folds), isotonic recalibration lowered the mean log-loss of random forests on 18 of 30 datasets but that of HistGradientBoostingClassifier on only 4 of 30.

Kumar et al. (2019, Appendix G, Definition G.3) debias the binned l1 calibration error (ECE) by subtracting an estimated bias from the plug-in estimate: for each bin k they draw R_k from a normal distribution with mean equal to the bin's empirical label mean y_k and variance y_k(1 - y_k)/(n p_k), and they estimate the debiased error as the plug-in estimate minus (the expectation of sum_k p_k |s_k - R_k| minus the plug-in estimate), approximating that expectation by simulation.

Kumar et al. (2019) describe their debiased estimator for the l1 calibration error as a heuristic approach and leave guarantees for it open; their sample-complexity guarantees apply to the squared (l2) calibration error.
